title: The Burgess Shale preserves parts that usually decay
body: The Burgess Shale in the Canadian Rockies is known for fossils of soft-bodied marine animals. Impressions preserve details that a record made only of shells and bones would leave out.
takeaway: What survives as a fossil can determine which creatures we even know existed.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Canadian Rocky Mountain Parks
visual: a soft-bodied marine fossil picked out by light on a dark shale slab

title: A stony reef can be built by animals a few millimetres wide
body: NOAA puts the typical width of many stony coral polyps at about 1 to 3 millimetres. The polyps secrete calcium carbonate skeletons, which accumulate into the hard structure of the reef.
takeaway: A reef's size comes from small contributions repeated across many generations.
source: NOAA Ocean Service, What Is a Coral Reef Made Of?
visual: a close view of tiny coral polyps spread over a limestone reef

title: Eye lenses helped date Greenland sharks that lived for centuries
body: In 2016 researchers radiocarbon-dated the centres of eye lenses from 28 female Greenland sharks. The biggest shark, about 5 metres long, was estimated to be at least 272 years old at the lower end of the study's range.
takeaway: A tissue formed early in life can retain a chemical clue to when an animal was born.
visual: a Greenland shark swimming through dark cold water under a faint light
